lesson.topicTitle: Structure and functions in living organisms

specAnchors.text: understand that a balanced diet should include appropriate proportions of carbohydrate, protein, lipid, vitamins, minerals, water and dietary fibre

identify the sources and describe the functions of carbohydrate, protein, lipid (fats and oils), vitamins A, C and D, the mineral ions calcium and iron, water and dietary fibre as components of the diet
understand how energy requirements vary with activity levels, age and pregnancy

primer.text: You know food fuels the body and that different meals feel different. This lesson formalises that: what a balanced diet actually contains, what each dietary element does and where it comes from, how malnutrition damages health, and why a growing child, an athlete and an expectant mother all need different quantities.

modules.title: Balance, Malnutrition and Its Costs
sourceHeadings: The Importance of a Balanced Diet
Causes and effects of malnutrition table
modules.opening: A balanced diet serves every food group in the right proportion: carbohydrate, protein, lipid, dietary fibre, vitamins, mineral ions and water. Skew those proportions and malnutrition follows, bringing a recognisable set of health problems that the corpus table lays out cause by cause.
keyPoints: A balanced diet means all food groups present in correct proportions.
An unbalanced diet leads to malnutrition.
Malnutrition produces a range of human health problems.
The seven key groups are carbohydrate, protein, lipid, fibre, vitamins, minerals and water.
The malnutrition table pairs each dietary cause with its effect.

low.restatement: Right amounts of everything: that is balance; wrong amounts bring malnutrition.
low.analogy: An orchestra needs every section at the right volume — one blaring section ruins the piece.
low.examPointer: List all seven groups by name; naming six loses the mark.

medium.restatement: Balance is about proportion, not abundance — even healthful groups distort the diet in excess.
medium.analogy: A recipe ruined by too much of one good ingredient.
medium.examPointer: Expect a table-completion question pairing causes of malnutrition with effects.

modules.title: Dietary Elements and Energy Needs
modules.opening: Each dietary element has a defined function and source: carbohydrate for energy from bread and rice, protein for growth and repair from meat and pulses, lipid for insulation and storage, fibre for bulk, vitamins and minerals for health maintenance, and water for chemical reactions. Requirements then shift with age, activity and pregnancy.
keyPoints: Carbohydrate supplies energy from sources like bread, cereals, pasta and rice.
Protein drives growth and repair; meat, fish, eggs and pulses supply it.
Lipid insulates and stores energy; butter, oil and nuts provide it.
Calcium builds bones and teeth; vitamin D helps absorb calcium; iron feeds haemoglobin.
Children need more protein proportionally, and active people need more energy overall.
Pregnancy raises energy needs and adds calcium and iron for the developing fetus.

low.restatement: Every element has a function, a source list, and a deficiency disease.
low.analogy: A toolbox: each tool has a job and a place it lives.
low.examPointer: Learn element-function-source-deficiency as four linked facts per nutrient.

medium.restatement: Deficiency diseases name the failure: scurvy without vitamin C, rickets without vitamin D, anaemia without iron.
medium.analogy: A factory line stopping when one part runs out.
medium.examPointer: Pair each vitamin or mineral with its exact deficiency condition by name.

glossary.definition: A diet supplying every food group in the correct proportions.
The health problems that follow an unbalanced diet.
The iron-based pigment in red blood cells that carries oxygen.
The childhood bone-condition caused by severe vitamin D shortage.
